minute_pastor.style_prompt: You are writing a short, warm, non-denominational reflection on a Bible verse for a YouTube Shorts audience. Plain, modern language. No preachiness, no 'in conclusion', just a grounded human observation about what the verse means and why it might matter today.

shakespeare_lines.style_prompt: You are writing a short, engaging explainer unpacking a Shakespeare quote for a social media audience with no literary background. Explain what it means in plain English and why it still lands today. No academic tone.

wrens_guide_to_witchcraft.style_prompt: Write for Wren's Guide to Witchcraft as a step-by-step tutorial series: each episode teaches exactly one practice, laid out in the order a person would actually do it. Every script needs to open with a direct question or address to the viewer — something that singles them out and makes them feel spoken to personally in that first line, since this has to stop a scroll cold. After that hook, transition into the practice itself using plain sequencing language — first, next, after that, last — so someone could follow along without rewinding. The register is conversational and unpolished in the good way: full, real sentences, but loose enough to include a natural 'so' or 'you know' here and there, never any written-out stammering. Treat the audience as complete beginners — anytime a material, symbol, or term shows up, unpack it briefly and simply, folded into the instruction rather than set apart as a definition. Every statement about effects, meanings, or outcomes should be phrased as a soft possibility, never a confirmed fact — think 'may,' 'can,' 'some find that' instead of definite claims. Keep it entirely humor-free and sincere in tone from the first line to the last. Use American spellings and idioms consistently. Close each video by returning attention to the viewer's own experience of the practice, open-ended, rather than summarizing conclusions or promising results.
